sections.h2: How does an eviction work in New Jersey from complaint to removal?
sections.html:
A landlord files a landlord-tenant complaint in the Special Civil Part of the Superior Court, wins a judgment for possession, then asks the court for a warrant of removal that a court officer carries out. No one else can lawfully put a residential tenant out, and the NJ Courts landlord-tenant page says any other attempt is illegal.

The case is heard in the county courthouse where the rental sits. A landlord who is a corporation, LLC or limited partnership must be represented by a New Jersey attorney. A sole proprietor or general partnership may file without one, though the court calls a lawyer a good idea.

The whole sequence usually takes longer than the statutory minimums suggest, since the tenant can ask for settlement time, a hardship stay or a later hearing. A house sale scheduled around an occupied rental should leave room for that.

sections.h2: What are the steps, fees and waiting periods?
sections.html:
The table lays out the court-set steps and the numbers published by NJ Courts.

Special Civil Part steps and timing, from the NJ Courts landlord-tenant self-help page
StepWhat the court page says
Filing the complaint$50 for one defendant, $5 for each added defendant, plus a $7 service fee
Trial dateAt least 21 days after the summons is served
Judgment for possessionTenant has three business days to pay rent and approved costs and stop the eviction
Warrant of removal$35 plus mileage; cannot issue until three business days after judgment
Notice to leaveResidential tenant gets at least three business days after the warrant is served
Landlord deadlinesApply for the warrant within 30 days of judgment; execute it within 30 days of issuance unless stayed

The officer's own eviction fee may not exceed $75, according to the same page, and the landlord pays that and any second mileage fee directly.

sections.h2: What does a landlord have to file with the complaint?
sections.html:
The packet is longer than many owners expect. The NJ Courts kit asks for the verified complaint, a tenancy summons, and a Landlord Case Information Statement, plus a copy of the lease.

  • Lease provisions that treat fees and charges as additional rent, and any rental assistance notice or eviction-ground clauses.
  • A Registration Statement and a Certification of Lease and Registration Statement, unless the property is exempt under N.J.S.A. 46:8-27.
  • For any case other than unpaid rent, every notice sent to the tenant or housing authority that will be used at trial.

The court page explains the registration rule. A landlord who lives on the property with three units or fewer registers with the municipal Community Development Authority, while other rentals register with the state Bureau of Housing Inspection. A missing registration can become a defense.

sections.h2: What happens at the trial date?
sections.html:
Both sides must show up. If the landlord does not appear, the case is dismissed, and if the tenant does not appear, the court marks the case as a default and the landlord can apply for judgment.

When both appear, trained court staff first try to settle the matter. A settlement might give the tenant more time to move or set a payment plan, and a judge must review and approve it for residential cases involving a tenant without a lawyer. If there is no deal, the judge hears the case and either grants or denies a judgment for possession.

The tenant cannot answer in writing. The court page says the defendant must come in person, and witnesses must testify live because signed statements are not accepted.

sections.h2: How can a tenant stop or delay an eviction?
sections.html:
The court lists several tools, and each one can change a seller's timeline.

  • Pay in full: in a nonpayment case the tenant can pay all rent plus allowed costs before or at trial, or up to three business days after the eviction, and the landlord must accept it. The page notes a $500 penalty if a landlord refuses or fails to tell the court.
  • Orderly removal: an order giving up to seven more calendar days to move.
  • Hardship stay: up to six months, but only if the tenant pays everything owed and keeps paying rent during the stay.
  • Vacate the judgment: a request the court says is not granted often.

The FAQ section on the same page adds that the orderly removal and hardship requests must be made within 10 days of the eviction date. Payment from a charity or rental assistance program must also be accepted by the landlord.

sections.h2: What defenses can a tenant raise?
sections.html:
New Jersey courts hear several common defenses, and each can stall a sale plan that assumes a quick removal. The NJ Courts site lists them.

  • Habitability: the Marini Doctrine lets a tenant withhold rent over problems like no heat or hot water, mold, rodents or a broken toilet, but only by depositing rent with the court and showing the landlord had a chance to fix it. It cannot excuse late payment patterns or noise violations.
  • Unregistered rental: no registration statement can sink the filing.
  • Illegal tenancy: a condemned property or an unapproved extra unit.
  • Abatement: the judge can reduce rent owed because of a defect.
  • Subsidy notice: a landlord must tell any public agency paying part of the rent, and the case can be dismissed if it did not.

sections.h2: What counts as an illegal lockout in New Jersey?
sections.html:
Any removal without a judgment for possession and a warrant carried out by a Special Civil Part officer. The court page names changing the locks, padlocking the doors, and shutting off gas, water or electricity as illegal ways to force a tenant out.

A landlord also cannot hold a tenant's furniture or belongings to force payment. A locked-out tenant can file in the Special Civil Part asking to be let back in and for damages.

This matters to anyone buying a rented house. A buyer who closes on an occupied property cannot clear it by self-help, and the same court process runs under the new owner's name. Back rent is a separate matter, since a judgment for possession does not award the unpaid amount and the landlord must sue for it in the special civil or small claims section.

sections.h2: How are renters treated when the house is in foreclosure or sold at sheriff's sale?
sections.html:
A tenant with a valid lease who is in good standing is generally not forced out because of foreclosure. The NJ Courts foreclosure self-help page points renters to the Anti-Eviction statute, N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 to 61.12, and tells them to consult an attorney if served with a complaint and to give the lender's attorney a copy of the lease.

The landlord-tenant page says the purchaser at a sheriff's sale takes the building subject to tenants' rights. Tenants should also receive the court's Notice to Residential Tenants of Rights During Foreclosure.

The foreclosure page describes how the court process runs: a 30-day notice of intent, a 35-day window to answer a complaint, and a sheriff's sale that must happen within 150 days of the writ of execution. After the sale the debtor has 10 days to redeem. An owner with a tenant in the house and a mortgage in trouble can use that period to arrange a sale instead.

sections.h2: What are the options for selling a New Jersey house that has a tenant?
sections.html:
There are three practical routes. Which one fits depends on the lease, the number of units and whether the tenant cooperates.

  • Sell with the tenant in place: the buyer takes over the tenancy, and the security deposit information must be updated in writing after a transfer.
  • Negotiate a move-out: a written agreement with the tenant, ideally reviewed by the court if a case is pending.
  • Use a recognized ground: a building of three units or fewer can be cleared for an owner or buyer who will live there, after two months' notice and once the lease ends.

After the tenant leaves, personal property left behind falls under New Jersey's abandoned property statute, which the court page says a landlord should check with an attorney before handling.

faqs.q: Can a New Jersey landlord change the locks to evict a tenant?
faqs.a: No. Changing locks, padlocking doors or cutting off utilities is an illegal lockout. Only a Special Civil Part officer can carry out an eviction, and only after a judgment for possession and a warrant of removal.

faqs.q: How long after a judgment does a tenant have to move out in New Jersey?
faqs.a: At least three business days after the warrant of removal is served. The warrant itself cannot issue until three business days after the judgment, so the minimum from judgment to eviction is about a week of business days.

faqs.q: Can a tenant stop an eviction by paying the back rent?
faqs.a: Yes, in nonpayment cases. Paying all rent due plus approved costs before or on the hearing date, or within three business days after the eviction, leads to dismissal, and the landlord must accept cash, a cashier's check or a money order.

faqs.q: Does a foreclosure automatically end a tenant's lease in New Jersey?
faqs.a: No. According to NJ Courts, a tenant with a valid lease in good standing is not forced to move just because the property is in foreclosure, and the sheriff's sale buyer takes the building subject to the tenant's rights.

faqs.q: Do I need a lawyer to evict a tenant in New Jersey?
faqs.a: Only if the landlord is a corporation, LLC or limited partnership. Individual owners and sole proprietors can file on their own, but the court recommends getting a lawyer if you can.
